Fig. 1:Overview of RoboCasa-Shift.RoboCasa-Shift evaluates VLA robustness on selected long-horizon RoboCasa tasks under controlled single-factor distribution shifts with multiple frozen severity levels.
Strictly matched clean-perturbed rollouts enable counterfactual comparison under shared task conditions, while robustness is characterized jointly through end-to-end task outcomes and stage-aware semantic execution diagnostics.
Representative findings illustrate that aggregate success rates can mask substantial episode-level outcome changes, similar end-to-end degradation can correspond to different failure locations, and severe visual corruption can shift failures toward earlier stages of task execution.

Fig. 2:Pipeline of RoboCasa-Shift.(a) Task Suite. Candidate RoboCasa tasks are filtered through clean-competence screening to construct the formal evaluation suite.
(b) Controlled Shifts. Selected tasks are evaluated under four single-factor distribution shifts with calibrated and frozen severity levels.
(c) Counterfactual Pairing. Clean and perturbed rollouts share the underlying task conditions and policy seed and differ only in the target shift.
(d) Diagnosis. RoboCasa’s official task outcome is complemented by stage-aware semantic diagnostics of execution progress, first incomplete subgoal, and subgoal reach.

Fig. 3:Overview of StageTracker.(a) A long-horizon task is represented as an ordered sequence of semantic subgoals, each associated with a simulator-state predicate.
(b) During rollout, StageTracker evaluates the current predicate, records the completion step when it is first satisfied, and advances to the next subgoal. Completed subgoals are latched, allowing the tracker to report the deepest semantic progress reached and the first incomplete subgoal for failure localization.

Fig. 4:End-to-end robustness under controlled distribution shifts.Macro-averaged paired success-rate degradationΔ​SR\Delta\mathrm{SR}is shown for the four distribution-shift factors, with each factor evaluated at three frozen severity levels (L1L_{1}–L3L_{3}). Positive values indicate degradation relative to the matched clean condition. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals obtained from paired bootstrap resampling. Severity levels are ordinal within each perturbation factor, and equal level indices across different factors do not imply physically equivalent perturbation magnitudes.

Fig. 5:Task-level robustness under controlled distribution shifts.Each cell reports the paired success-rate degradationΔ​SR\Delta\mathrm{SR}for one task and perturbation condition, computed from 20 matched episode pairs. Positive values indicate degradation relative to the matched clean condition, while negative values indicate a higher success rate under the shifted condition for the corresponding finite paired sample. The task-level breakdown reveals heterogeneous severity responses that can be obscured by macro aggregation.

Fig. 7:Representative matched replays at different semantic failure depths.Each case compares a strictly matched clean–perturbed rollout pair that shares the same task instance, initial simulator state, episode metadata,
and episode-level policy seed, while differing only in the target perturbation. The two rows show the clean and perturbed executions, respectively, and the columns present selected frames spanning the execution process.
Checkmarks and crosses indicate whether the corresponding tracked semantic subgoals are completed, while the final annotation reports the official task outcome. These examples provide a qualitative view of how perturbations can change execution depth and
failure location, complementing the aggregate stage-aware statistics in
Figure6.
